name: Ann Widdecombe
role: British Conservative MP (1987–2010), prisons minister and shadow home secretary; Brexit Party MEP (2019–2020); Reform UK spokesperson
summary: A social conservative and committed Catholic, Widdecombe opposed abortion, assisted dying and equal treatment of same-sex relationships in law, and backed the death penalty and tough drugs enforcement. She was a leading Eurosceptic who left the Conservatives for the Brexit Party and later served as Reform UK's immigration and justice spokesperson, favouring lower immigration.

legalize-drugs.rationale: In December 2002 she said she held strong disapproval of the Home Secretary's decision to reclassify cannabis, and in May 2008 welcomed the Government's U-turn and called the years since downgrading a wasted opportunity, urging fixed penalty fines as a deterrent.

reviewHistory.rationale: As shadow Home Secretary she used her 2000 Conservative conference speech to call for zero tolerance of cannabis use, with £100 fines for users.

rehabilitation.rationale: As prisons minister, and in later remarks, she said prisons should prepare people for law-abiding lives through work and education and that redemption is possible, but also insisted prison must not be comfortable and defended punishment; evidence points both ways.

traditional-family.rationale: On 30 March 2010 she told the House of record levels of family break-up and children growing up in split households, and drew attention to the plight of parents in a committed marriage, especially the non-working mother who stays home, who wish to bring children up in a stable environment.

reviewHistory.rationale: Argued the state must have a preferred model of marriage, a union generally open to procreation, and said homosexuality could not be promoted as an equally valid lifestyle to marriage.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: In the Civil Partnership Bill debate of 9 November 2004 she said she would have preferred to address the injustices through other legislation rather than set up a situation in which no discernible difference exists between a civil marriage and a civil partnership, 'that is why it is so wrong'; in 2009 she said it is against Catholic teaching to recognise homosexual unions as equivalent to marriage.

reviewHistory.rationale: Opposed same-sex marriage, arguing the state must have a preferred model of marriage generally open to procreation; she did not, however, back abolishing it once introduced.

abortion-legal.rationale: In the Commons on 20 May 2008, opposing a clause to change the law on abortion, she argued that the logic of the case for no restrictions is abortion on demand right up to birth, and she sat among the free-vote opponents in the Human Fertilisation and Embryology Bill debates.

reviewHistory.rationale: Opposed the legality of abortion throughout her parliamentary career; as shadow health secretary in 1998 she said she would not take the Health Secretary post while it carried responsibility for abortions.

reduce-immigration.rationale: As Reform UK immigration spokesperson (2024) said legal and illegal migration must be cut to sustainable levels because of its effects on housing, health services, wages and the economy.

national-self-determination.rationale: Her 2019 European Parliament maiden speech likened Brexit to a colony rising against occupiers; she campaigned for the UK to govern itself outside the EU.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Spoke of a gap between a metropolitan elite and the red wall and said people feel betrayed by politicians; did not specifically say elites are corrupt.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Prominent Eurosceptic: backed Vote Leave and sat as a Brexit Party MEP; said Britain had been "completely subservient to EU law" and wanted to be close to the EU but "not ruled by them".

death-penalty.rationale: Repeatedly backed reintroducing the death penalty; in a 2024 interview said she remained firmly of that view and that it should be available to courts for premeditated murder, not automatic.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: In the Animal Welfare Bill debate of 6 November 2006 she said she shared the view that it is a most important Bill that people with an interest in animal welfare will welcome, and criticised the decision not to ban pet fairs, while in 2007 she opposed the Hunting Act's enforcement being lax and wanted hunts monitored.

reviewHistory.rationale: Supported rigorous animal protection laws and consistently voted for the fox hunting ban, including opposing amendment of the Hunting Act in 2015.

notes: Wikipedia states she was found dead at her Devon home on 9 July 2026 (death c. 8 July), so living is false. Her prisons-minister papers and Strictly Ann texts could not be reached (not in an open page; her Commons speeches are now read); several topics (economy, welfare, tax, trade, most culture questions) have no sourced position and are null. On the Commons she took the opposing side on 15 of 17 LGBT-equality votes per Public Whip as reported by Wikipedia. Later pass 2026-11-13 (rules 7): sources tagged by evidence; her Commons Hansard (1987-2010) is searched by theme and answers seven statements that rested on Wikipedia; three Wikipedia-only answers with no support in Hansard are nulled.
